research.title: Patient-Facing AI System for Symptom Guidance Using Simulated Encounters and Physician Review: Analytical Validation Study
research.finding: Verily Health analytically validated its LLM-based Personal Health Assistant (PHA) for symptom guidance using 772 synthetic cases generated from published telephone-triage protocols and LLM-assisted persona-based generation. Five independent physicians reviewed each case without access to PHA outputs to establish ground-truth level-of-care recommendations. PHA met the prespecified overtriage criterion (11.0%, criterion <30%) but did not meet the urgent undertriage criterion (6.9%, criterion <5%) or the nonurgent undertriage criterion (18.4%, criterion <15%). Undertriage was identified as the principal performance gap requiring further product refinement. Secondary analyses found PHA-generated possible conditions, self-care recommendations, and lab-testing recommendations were generally clinically appropriate. PHA was based on the OpenAI GPT-5.4-mini LLM (2026-03-17 release).
research.caveat: The study used synthetic cases, simulated conversations, and enriched urgency categories under controlled conditions; results may not reflect real-world performance. The authors explicitly state that prospective evaluation with actual users is needed before broader clinical use. The study was conducted by Verily employees (conflicts of interest) and the PHA configuration was locked before evaluation, so results may not reflect the current product.

research.title: The Anatomy of a Personal Health Agent
research.finding: A comprehensive personal health agent reasoning over multimodal consumer device and medical record data, built as three specialist sub-agents: a data science agent analysing longitudinal wearable and medical data with population-level context, a health domain expert agent integrating personal and contextual data with health knowledge, and a health coach agent synthesising insights, supporting multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applying psychological strategies and tracking progress. Four user journeys guided the design: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice and symptom assessment. Evaluated across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and about 1,350 hours of effort from health experts and end users. Released as an open-source multi-agent framework. Validated for real-world applicability against the WEAR-ME metabolic health study (n=1,165).
research.caveat: Independent reporting noted safety gaps in a meaningful share of generated summaries, and the authors present the work as a basis for further research rather than a deployable clinical tool.

research.title: Transforming Wearable Data into Personal Health Insights Using LLM Agents
research.finding: Argues that making sense of wearable streams requires complex numerical reasoning beyond conventional language models and introduces an LLM agent that iterates over tools and longitudinal data to produce wearable-derived health insights.
research.caveat: Consumer sensor data quality and device heterogeneity remain open problems; insights are not clinical conclusions.

research.title: Using AI to Offer Personalised Health Advice
research.finding: Companion editorial placing the personal health agent paper in the wider context of public trust in AI health information, citing Pew survey research and prior studies on AI-delivered health advice.
research.caveat: Editorial commentary, not primary evidence.

research.title: Check Symptoms & Get Care: Mount Sinai's AI Triage Solution
research.finding: Digital triage deployment handling roughly 22,000 patient sessions, with about 80% of users who started completed the conversation. Blinded clinician comparison and continuous post-deployment review showed 88% to 96% concordance with physician triage, with a tiered adoption roadmap for organisations of different sizes.
research.caveat: Single health-system deployment; concordance is not the same as outcome improvement, and the authors describe a staged roadmap rather than a finished evaluation.

research.title: Symptom Checker Triage Accuracy: What a Decade of Research Shows
research.finding: Top-performing AI symptom checkers reached roughly 82-88% accuracy at assigning the correct level of care across 500 clinical vignettes in one multi-platform evaluation. A broader 2026 analysis of 22 ChatGPT versions found a consistent tendency across models to overtriage rather than undertriage.
research.caveat: Vignette studies overstate real-world performance; overtriage consumes clinical capacity even though it is the safer error direction.

research.title: Reliability of LLMs as Medical Assistants for the General Public: A Randomized Preregistered Study
research.finding: The largest randomised user study of LLMs for consumer medical advice tested GPT-4o, Llama 3 and Command R+ with 1,298 UK participants across 10 medical scenarios. LLMs alone correctly identified conditions in 94.9% of cases and chose the right disposition in 56.3% on average. But participants using the same LLMs identified conditions in fewer than 34.5% of cases and chose the right action in fewer than 44.2% - no better than a control group using ordinary search or their own judgement. The gap traced to two-way communication breakdown: users omitted information the model needed, and responses combined good and poor recommendations. The authors conclude that standard benchmarks for medical knowledge and simulated patient interactions do not predict failures with human users, and recommend systematic human user testing before public deployment in healthcare.
research.caveat: Ten scenarios is a narrow scope; the study uses simulated medical scenarios rather than real symptoms, and three LLMs may not generalise to all consumer health agents. The 56.3% disposition accuracy for LLMs alone is close to the 55-60% triage accuracy of older symptom checkers, suggesting the gap is in the user interaction, not the medical knowledge.

research.title: AI Triage Validation Across Three Swedish Emergency Departments
research.finding: An AI triage system validated on nearly 3,000 real-world emergency department cases outperformed junior clinicians at identifying patients requiring emergency care across multiple clinical scenarios.
research.caveat: Vitals-based scoring complements rather than replaces clinical assessment; emergency populations differ from consumer symptom-checker users.

research.title: FDA Relaxes Clinical Decision Support and General Wellness Guidance
research.finding: The FDA announced sweeping changes to digital health oversight, easing regulation of AI-enabled devices and wearables and revising general wellness and CDS guidance, while keeping software involving medical image or in vitro diagnostic signal processing in the device category. The agency signalled substantial cuts to existing digital health guidance and a new AI framework.
research.caveat: The relaxation widens the wellness lane for consumer agents while making the wellness-versus-medical-claim boundary the decisive compliance question.

research.title: 2026 Privacy Reset: State Law, Consent and the Post-HIPAA Gap
research.finding: California and Washington now require detailed written consent for AI tools processing health data, and Colorado's SB 21-169 imposes obligations on developers and deployers of high-risk AI in insurance. HIPAA sets the floor for covered entities; consumer health agents outside that scope face the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule plus a patchwork of stricter state law.
research.caveat: State requirements are moving faster than federal guidance; compliance depends on the residency of users and the flow of data.

research.title: Copilot Conversation Analysis: Health Demand in General Assistants
research.finding: Microsoft's analysis of more than 500,000 de-identified Copilot conversations from January 2026 found nearly one in five involved personal symptom assessment or condition discussion, evidencing how much health demand already flows through general-purpose assistants.
research.caveat: Vendor-reported, de-identified sample; classification method and generalisability are not independently verified.

research.title: HealthClaw: A Self-Evolving Agent for Longitudinal Personal Health Management
research.finding: Introduces HealthClaw, an open-source agent architecture that separates shared safety rules and medical knowledge (L0 - L1) from private longitudinal memory (L2 profile, L3 procedures, L4 episodic traces). After each interaction, an induction step decides what to update, revise, keep as episodic, or exclude. Across 900 longitudinal support probes on a synthetic year-long benchmark, answer accuracy increased from 0.2% with current-query prompting to 45.7% with HealthClaw, while prompt-side context exposure was 71.7% lower than full-history prompting. In 100 privacy probes, HealthClaw produced higher privacy-aware answer quality and fewer unsafe disclosures than both baselines. Nine 200-case biomedical tasks showed a mean absolute gain of 27.0 percentage points, with seven gains significant after FDR correction. Code publicly available on GitHub.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. All headline metrics come from automated rubric evaluators (Qwen-3.7-based) with no human-rated validation; if the evaluator is systematically lenient, accuracy and privacy gaps may be overstated. The benchmark is synthetic; clinical effectiveness requires prospective evaluation.

research.title: SensorFM and the Shift from Metrics to Agents
research.finding: Google's SensorFM, trained on roughly a trillion minutes of wearable data, supports the shift from raw metrics toward AI health agents. The analysis frames the core user problem quantitatively: people do not know what to do with hundreds of daily data points, they want actionable interpretation, which is why Oura and WHOOP moved to two-way coaching.
research.caveat: Industry analysis and vendor data; no independent outcome study of coaching effectiveness is cited.

research.title: The Health AI Agent Rush: Five Products in Three Months
research.finding: A comparative analysis of five health AI products (OpenAI ChatGPT Health, Anthropic Claude for Healthcare, Amazon Health AI, Microsoft Copilot Health, Perplexity Health) across 16 dimensions found all five launched between January and March 2026 with a remarkably similar model: EHR integration via intermediaries (b.well, HealthEx), wearable connections, no-training commitments, US-only availability, and separate storage from ordinary chat. None meets the full 'sealed mode' privacy standard (cryptographic hardening, human access constraints, independent verification). None is HIPAA-covered. All exclude European users, bundling privacy protections with data integration features in a way that denies Europeans both. OpenAI reports 230 million people ask ChatGPT health questions weekly.
research.caveat: The analysis is authored by a single researcher proposing a governance framework ('sealed mode'); product architectures are assessed from public materials, not independent audits, and may have changed since publication.

research.title: States Continue Efforts to Regulate AI in Healthcare: 2026 Legislation Review
research.finding: A review of 2026 state legislation found states leading Congress on health AI governance. Six states (AL, IN, UT, WA, MD, GA) enacted laws requiring human oversight of AI in insurer prior-authorisation decisions. Maine and Arizona restricted autonomous clinical decision-making in behavioural health and required informed consent for AI-powered tools. Four states (ID, NE, OR, TN) passed AI companion and chatbot safety acts requiring AI disclosure, crisis-response protocols for suicidal ideation, and prohibiting chatbots from representing themselves as licensed mental health professionals. Utah piloted a regulatory sandbox for AI-enabled prescription renewal under its AI Policy Act.
research.caveat: Legal analysis by a law firm; summarises enacted legislation and effective dates but does not assess enforcement capacity or practical impact on consumer health AI products.

research.title: Predicting Insulin Resistance from Wearable Data (Metwally et al.)
research.finding: A Google study of 1,165 US adults in the WEAR-ME cohort found that wearable-derived features (sleep, activity, heart rate) combined with demographics predicted insulin resistance (HOMA-IR > 2.9) with an AUROC of 0.70 (sensitivity 60%, specificity 80%). The work underpins the insulin resistance trends feature in Google's Health Guardian suite on Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air.
research.caveat: AUROC of 0.70 is modest; the model provides trend data only, not on-demand insulin or blood glucose levels. Google has not published accuracy figures for the shipping consumer feature, which is labelled general wellness.

research.title: Sex-Based Diagnostic Bias in AI Symptom Checkers
research.finding: A structured audit of three AI symptom checkers (Ada Health, Isabel Healthcare, Docus AI) across four clinical vignettes (ACS with chest pressure, ACS without chest pressure, pulmonary embolism, panic attack) found sex-based divergence in outputs from all three platforms, appearing as differences in differential diagnosis rank, probability estimates and advisory text. Isabel Healthcare ranked Heart Attack first for the male profile but third for the female profile on ACS with chest pressure. Docus AI assigned lower ACS probability to the female profile while its text described the presentation as common in women, and described immediate medical attention as crucial for the male profile but merely important for the female. The direction of divergence was not uniformly unfavorable to females.
research.caveat: Exploratory audit with four vignettes and three platforms; not a systematic evaluation of clinical safety. The authors call for equity auditing before and after deployment, with attention to both numerical outputs and generated explanatory text.

research.title: Consumer Health Data Privacy Patchwork Growing as Federal Enforcement Pulls Back
research.finding: The federal government has stepped back from enforcing HIPAA just as state legislatures accelerated privacy efforts, making compliance more fragmented. Connecticut, Maryland, Nevada and Washington enacted consumer health data privacy laws requiring consent before disclosing health data. Experts said patients voluntarily enter sensitive health information into consumer AI tools like ChatGPT without understanding the risks. CMS launched a Health Tech Ecosystem initiative as a voluntary, post-regulatory approach. No comprehensive federal solution is on the horizon.
research.caveat: Industry analysis quoting experts; not a systematic legal review. State laws are evolving rapidly and the article reflects a point-in-time snapshot.

research.title: Abbott-Google Partnership: Lingo CGM + Google Health AI for Metabolic Insights
research.finding: Abbott and Google announced a partnership pairing the Lingo consumer CGM with Google Health's AI to deliver personalised metabolic insights through the Google Health app. Lingo users can view glucose trends alongside other health metrics, with Google's Health Coach translating patterns into nutrition, activity and sleep recommendations. The companies also plan one of the largest real-world metabolic health studies, integrating CGM, wearable, lab and survey data to examine connections between daily behaviour and metabolic health.
research.caveat: Vendor announcement; the planned metabolic health study has no published protocol or results. The partnership is a commercial arrangement; effectiveness of AI-generated metabolic insights from CGM data has not been independently evaluated.

research.title: Privacy-Preserving Ambient Sensing for Activities of Daily Living: Multimodal Radar-Thermal Human Activity Recognition and Smart Plug Appliance Recognition
research.finding: NTU researchers developed a low-cost monitoring system combining mmWave radar, low-resolution thermal sensors and smart plugs to track daily routines and detect health emergencies in the home without cameras or wearables. AI learns individual behaviour patterns over time to identify anomalies such as falls, heart attacks, strokes or gradual deterioration in mobility. Tested in mock domestic environments with six room layouts, with multimodal sensor fusion outperforming any single sensor type. The privacy-by-design approach uses pixelated thermal sensors that identify posture without facial features, and smart-plug appliance patterns to infer daily activities like making tea or preparing food.
research.caveat: Laboratory mock-environment testing, not real-world deployment with actual older adults. The system's ability to distinguish genuine emergencies from normal routine variations in uncontrolled settings is unproven. Small evaluation scope with six room layouts.

research.title: BeST: Benchmark Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
research.venue: medRxiv (BeST Study Group, Central Research Institute of Ambulatory Health Care in Germany)
research.finding: The BeST study compared emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement across self-triage systems and multiple generations of OpenAI models against preliminary expert consensus. The evaluation addresses how triage outcomes differ across GPT model generations, providing quality assurance data for digital self-triage as adoption widens. Results show generational variation in triage safety and accuracy.
research.caveat: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. The expert consensus used as ground truth is preliminary. Vignette-based evaluation may not reflect real-world triage performance with actual patients.

research.title: Accuracy of a Respiratory Assessment Chatbot in a Nationwide Messaging System for Layperson Diagnosis and Triage
research.finding: A randomised preregistered study evaluated a respiratory assessment chatbot embedded in a nationwide messaging system for layperson diagnosis and triage. The study tested diagnostic and triage accuracy across respiratory symptoms in a real-world messaging deployment at population scale, providing evidence for chatbot-assisted respiratory self-assessment.
research.caveat: Single-condition focus (respiratory). Real-world messaging deployment may differ from clinical assessment settings. Generalisability to other condition categories is not established.

research.title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Personalised Health Checkup Interpretation and Guidance
research.finding: Presents a multi-agent LLM system that identifies multiple intents in health checkup questions, maps each to a task-specific agent, executes them in parallel, and synthesises outputs. Comparison of single-agent and multi-agent configurations found the multi-agent approach improved answer quality for complex health checkup interpretation requiring reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance and healthcare navigation.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Evaluation methodology and benchmark details not fully described in the abstract. Real-world health checkup data quality and heterogeneity may affect performance.

research.title: Technology-Enhanced Health Care in Smart Homes: Scoping Review of Sensor Technologies, Clinical Applications, Integration Challenges, and Future Directions
research.finding: A scoping review synthesising literature on technology-enhanced health care (TEH) integration within smart homes. Examines global deployment patterns, technological maturity, biomedical sensor integration, machine learning applications, and health outcomes. Covers the Internet of Medical Things, wearable biosensors and AI-driven analytics for proactive care delivery, particularly for older adults and individuals with chronic conditions living independently.
research.caveat: Scoping review, not systematic review or meta-analysis. Heterogeneous study designs and technologies make direct comparison difficult. Most included studies are early-stage deployments or pilots.

research.title: PIA: A Personal Intelligence Agent Turning Health Conversations into Records and Records into Understanding
research.finding: Introduces PIA, a personal intelligence agent that transforms health conversations into structured records and uses them for longitudinal understanding. Unlike general-purpose agent memory that summarises conversations into text snippets, PIA extracts structured health data (doses, trends, timelines) and retrieves by structured query rather than text similarity. The authors argue a health agent cannot run on summaries alone: a dose becomes a sentence, temporal references resolve at model discretion, and glucose trends cannot be answered by text similarity.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Evaluation details and performance metrics are not fully described in the abstract. Real-world deployment with actual patient health conversations is not demonstrated.

research.title: Patient Journey Evaluation for Consumer AI Health Assistants
research.finding: Defines a journey-level evaluation and governance framework for record-linked patient education by consumer AI health assistants. Introduces the personal health workspace (PHW), a user-controlled setting for evaluating an assistant as a stateful system across a patient journey rather than isolated Q&A turns. Includes a clinical journey map and an auditable interaction loop for testing longitudinal reliability before deployment and monitoring afterward.
research.caveat: Perspective article proposing a framework, not an empirical study. The PHW concept has not been validated in a real-world deployment. Feasibility and scalability of the proposed evaluation loop are not demonstrated.

research.title: SAFE-CARE Bench: A Benchmark Specification and Evaluation Protocol for Safety, Guardrails, and User Experience in Multi-Turn Healthcare AI Agent Conversations
research.finding: SAFE-CARE Bench tests what a healthcare AI agent does across a conversation, where risk builds turn by turn and a missed escalation is the failure that matters most. A controlled A0 - A4 ablation runs five agent variants over identical simulated conversations, with model, temperature and seed held constant. Each tier declares capability flags explicitly so any two tiers diff mechanically and every score change is attributable to a named capability bundle: grounding, safety guardrails, personalisation or agency.
research.caveat: Benchmark specification, not an empirical study with reported results. Simulated conversations may not capture the full range of real-world user behaviour. The framework has not been independently validated against clinical outcomes.

research.title: Are Frontier Large Language Models Safer Than Government-Backed Symptom Checkers for Clinical Self-Triage? A Standardised Vignette Evaluation
research.finding: Compared Australia's Healthdirect symptom checker (2.4 million uses in FY2024-25) against six LLM configurations across triage accuracy and safety using standardised vignettes. The first evaluation of a government-backed symptom checker against frontier large language models, and the first to explore whether premium LLM subscriptions improve triage safety.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Vignette-based evaluation may not reflect real-world triage performance. Single government-backed symptom checker; generalisability to other national systems is not established.

research.title: Authentication Status and AI Triage Concordance Among Care Seekers in a US Health System
research.finding: A prospective cohort analysis of 6,772 care seekers using an AI triage tool at a US health system found that users' pre-stated care intent aligned with AI recommendations differently depending on authentication status, and that alignment shaped downstream engagement. The study addresses how user identity and stated intent affect the reliability of AI triage tools deployed at the digital front door of health systems.
research.caveat: Single health-system study. Concordance between pre-stated intent and AI recommendation is not the same as triage correctness. The study does not report clinical outcomes downstream of triage.

research.title: SymptomAI: Toward a Conversational AI Agent for Everyday Symptom Assessment
research.finding: Google Research deployed SymptomAI, a set of conversational AI agents for end-to-end patient interviewing and differential diagnosis, via the Fitbit app in a study randomising N=13,917 participants across five AI agent configurations. A subset of 1,228 participants reported a clinician-provided diagnosis, and 517 were further evaluated by a panel of clinicians during over 250 hours of annotation. SymptomAI's differential diagnoses were significantly more accurate than independent clinicians given the same dialogue (OR=2.56, p<0.001) in a blinded randomised comparison. Agentic strategies conducting a dedicated symptom interview that elicits additional information before providing a diagnosis substantially outperformed user-guided conversations (p<0.001). An auxiliary analysis on 1,509 conversations from a general US population panel validated generalisability beyond wearable users. SymptomAI diagnoses were used as labels to analyse over 500,000 days of wearable metrics across nearly 400 conditions, identifying strong associations between acute infections and physiological shifts (e.g., OR>7 for influenza).
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Ground truth is self-reported clinician diagnoses for a subset, not uniformly verified. The study is by Google Research employees (potential conflict of interest). The OR=2.56 comparison against clinicians is based on the same dialogue text, not independent patient encounters, so it measures diagnostic accuracy from transcript rather than clinical performance.

research.title: RubricsTree: Scalable and Evolving Open-Ended Evaluation of Personal Health Agents across Health Memory and Medical Skills
research.finding: Introduces RubricsTree, a scalable evaluation framework with an expert-aligned hierarchical taxonomy of over 100 atomic, clinically-verifiable Boolean rubrics, evolved from 4,000 real user queries through an iterative human-in-the-loop curation protocol led by an experienced physician. A context-aware adaptive router activates only the relevant auto-weighted rubric subset per query. When used as structured instructions, text feedback, or training rewards for performance optimisation, RubricsTree yields up to ~66% relative gains on HealthBench for Gemini, GPT, and Qwen model families. The framework addresses the bottleneck where physician annotation is reliable but costly, while LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are scalable but subjective and sometimes clinically misaligned.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The framework is developed by Google Research employees (potential conflict of interest). HealthBench gains are self-reported and may not generalise to other benchmarks or clinical settings. The rubrics are derived from 4,000 user queries, which may not cover the full spectrum of personal health agent interactions.

research.title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
research.finding: Presents ECHO (Enhanced Care & Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop with LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory, achieving 94.9% tool-execution pass rate across 59 scenarios with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer combines rule-based crisis detection (sub-1ms) with a signed graph neural network achieving 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query Turkish health dataset, outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech module estimates emotion, depression, and pain (macro F1=0.652). The full system runs on consumer hardware with no external data transmission, supporting GDPR/KVKK compliance.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The safety evaluation is on a Turkish-language dataset, which may limit generalisability to other languages and clinical contexts. The 59-scenario benchmark is small. The speech assessment F1 of 0.652 is modest and may not be reliable enough for clinical use.

research.title: SuperSenseDoctor: A Multimodal and Contactless Agent for Health Tracking
research.finding: Presents a multimodal contactless agent architecture for long-term home health tracking, transforming WiFi, mmWave radar, and surface temperature into a persistent human health state. The system uses fixed decision rules for daily monitoring and event-driven reasoning for anomalies, integrating sensing, temporal state, reasoning, and action into an auditable loop. The calibrated pipeline achieves 1.994 bpm MAE for heart rate, 0.197 bpm MAE for respiratory rate, 96.5% fall-recognition accuracy, and 96.7% criterion-level checklist pass rate across 2,686 one-second states.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Laboratory evaluation only, not tested in real-world home environments with actual older adults. The system's ability to distinguish genuine emergencies from routine variations in uncontrolled settings is unproven. Small evaluation scope.

research.title: Separating Safety from Preference in Clinical LLM Evaluation
research.venue: ACM 4th International Workshop on Human-Centered Sensing, Modeling, and Intelligent Systems
research.finding: A human-centered evaluation of the mRehab Advisory Agent with two cohorts: six domain experts rating clinical safety and correctness, and three end users rating helpfulness, affect, and clarity, alongside blinded best-to-worst rankings. In a 200-question pilot (435 ranked triples), raters ranked the agent first most often (53.3%, p<0.001), yet it led on affect and clarity, not helpfulness, and drew mixed safety verdicts. The study demonstrates that a fluent, well-liked answer can still be clinically unsafe, and that preference-only evaluation hides this by collapsing many judgments into one winner. Provenance-rich ranking records enable post-hoc analysis of disagreements.
research.caveat: Small pilot study with 200 questions, six experts and three end users. The mRehab Advisory Agent is a specific system; generalisability to other consumer health agents is not established. The workshop paper format limits detail on methodology.

research.title: Safety Evaluation of a Generative AI Agent for Anxiety and Depression Symptoms
research.finding: Evaluates the safety of a clinician-designed generative AI care agent for anxiety and depression symptoms using a scalable dual-methods paradigm: high-throughput in silico simulation paired with continuous real-world monitoring. The digital program delivered structured cognitive behavioural skills training through the AI agent. The evaluation addresses the challenge that conventional one-off evaluation approaches cannot fully address the probabilistic nature and rapid model iteration of generative AI in mental health, where model updates can change safety behaviour. An exploratory aim assessed preliminary within-person symptom reduction.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The specific AI agent and its clinical configuration are not fully described in the abstract. In silico simulation may not capture all real-world safety risks. Symptom reduction findings are exploratory.

research.title: Safety, Hallucination, and Failure Modes in Agentic Health AI: A State-of-the-Art Review
research.finding: A systematic literature review of safety issues in agentic AI systems deployed in clinical environments. Unlike conventional single-turn AI tools, agentic systems autonomously plan multistep tasks, invoke external tools, retain memory across interactions, and pursue clinical goals with minimal human intervention, introducing a qualitatively distinct safety profile. The review covers hallucination, tool misuse, memory corruption, and escalation failures across radiology, clinical decision support, intensive care monitoring, drug discovery, and patient-facing care. The authors identify gaps in existing safety frameworks when applied to multi-turn, tool-using, memory-enabled health AI agents.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. As a review, it synthesises existing literature but does not present new empirical findings. The agentic AI safety field is nascent and the review may not capture all emerging failure modes.

research.title: Patient Safety and Health Equity of AI-Enabled Triage Tools in Primary Care: A Systematic Review
research.finding: A systematic review synthesising real-world patient safety evidence for AI-enabled triage tools in primary care. The review searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and Scopus (January 2015-November 2025) with citation searching, covering prospective studies evaluating AI triage tools in real-world primary care settings. The review maps whether safety has been examined across sociodemographic groups, addressing the gap between vignette-based validation and real-world safety evidence.
research.caveat: Systematic review of prospective studies; the quality and heterogeneity of included studies may limit generalisability. The review focuses on primary care settings, which may not generalise to emergency or specialist triage. The review period ends November 2025, so very recent tools may not be covered.

research.title: SCARF: Symptom Checker Accuracy Reporting Framework for Standardised Evaluation
research.finding: Proposes a standardised framework for evaluating symptom checkers and diagnostic decision support systems, addressing the lack of quality control in existing evaluation approaches. The framework responds to a decade of criticism of the vignette-based evaluation methodology introduced in 2015, providing a structured reporting standard for accuracy, safety, and performance metrics across symptom checker platforms.
research.caveat: Framework paper, not an empirical study. Adoption by symptom checker developers and researchers is voluntary. The framework has not been independently validated against clinical outcomes.

research.title: FDA Discussion Paper: Considerations for the Regulation of Generative AI-Enabled Medical Devices
research.venue: FDA Digital Health Center of Excellence
research.finding: The FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence published a discussion paper on considerations for regulating GenAI-enabled medical devices, covering risk assessment, premarket evaluation, postmarket monitoring, and other regulatory topics. The paper seeks stakeholder feedback on the unique risks posed by GenAI compared to traditional AI-enabled devices, including unpredictability of outputs, continuous learning, and broader use contexts. Feedback was accepted through October 19, 2026 via docket FDA-2026-N-7874. The paper is explicitly for discussion purposes only and does not represent draft or final guidance.
research.caveat: Discussion paper, not guidance. Does not represent FDA's proposed or final regulatory expectations. The paper does not address whether the approaches discussed are within FDA's existing legal authorities or whether new authorities would be necessary.

research.title: AI Symptom Checker Integrated Into MomConnect Maternal Healthcare Platform
research.finding: A prospective observational mixed-methods study evaluated an AI-based symptom checker integrated into South Africa's MomConnect maternal healthcare platform, examining the symptom checker's integration, usage patterns and performance within a national digital health messaging system for maternal health. It provides real-world evidence for AI symptom assessment in a public health context at national scale.
research.caveat: Observational mixed-methods evaluation of integration, usage and performance - not a randomised accuracy validation, and it does not establish that the symptom checker outperforms clinical triage or a non-AI pathway. Single national programme, so generalisation to other health systems or populations is untested.

research.title: California Extends CMIA Privacy Protections to Consumer Health Care Chatbots
research.finding: California enacted AB 1979, extending the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act (CMIA) to businesses offering consumer-facing health care chatbots. From January 1, 2027, companies providing chatbots for managing health information, or for diagnosis, treatment or management of a medical condition, will be deemed health care providers under CMIA and must maintain the same confidentiality standards as providers. The law also limits how health care providers may use AI in clinical care. It is the first state law to explicitly bring consumer health AI chatbots under medical privacy protections equivalent to those covering providers.
research.caveat: Law-firm analysis of enacted legislation, not the statutory text itself. Implementation and enforcement from January 1, 2027 remain unobserved, and the analysis does not address how a chatbot is distinguished from an ordinary consumer wellness app in practice.

research.title: AI Health Coaches Compared: Four Wearable Platforms, Four Price Points
research.finding: A market comparison of four wearable platforms selling AI health coaches in 2026: Google Health Coach at $9.99/month, WHOOP Coach included in memberships from $199/year, Oura Advisor included at $5.99/month, and Garmin Active Intelligence at $6.99/month, with Apple still shipping no AI coach. It frames the competitive shift in the category: in 2024 the pitch was more sensors, in 2026 it is a chatbot that reads them for you, with every major wearable platform now selling an AI coach that ingests sleep, strain and heart data and tells users what to do about it.
research.caveat: Vendor-published market comparison of list prices - not a clinical evaluation, and no product quality is assessed. Prices are as published by the vendor and may not reflect current or promotional pricing, and inclusion in a membership bundle is not directly comparable to a standalone subscription.

research.title: Google's End-to-End Evaluation Framework for Health AI
research.finding: Google Research, in partnership with Dr. Elizabeth McGlynn and Dr. Dana Gelb Safran, published a whitepaper detailing an end-to-end evaluation approach to assess AI use cases for health needs. The framework evaluates models across three areas: accuracy, safety, and usefulness, combining closed-question benchmarks, autoraters, and expert human review to assess common and high-risk health scenarios.
research.caveat: Whitepaper from Google Research (vendor conflict of interest). The framework has not been independently validated. Specific model performance results are not provided in the blog post summary.

research.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
research.finding: Presents DiabAgent, an agentic system for physiological control in diabetes management that extends medical LLMs from answering questions to taking actions that influence physiology. The work represents a shift from advisory AI to agentic intervention, where the system does not just recommend but acts on health parameters.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The system is a research prototype and has not been validated in clinical trials. Agentic physiological control raises safety questions distinct from advisory systems.

research.title: When AI Becomes a Medical Device: FDA Boundaries for Patient-Facing Health Tools
research.finding: Legal analysis examining how the FDA evaluates AI health software based on intended use and functionality. Attorneys explain how to design AI features that preserve clinicians' independent judgment and support exclusion from device regulation, and when patient-facing tools may trigger FDA oversight.
research.caveat: Legal analysis by practitioners, not regulatory guidance from FDA itself. The analysis reflects the regulatory landscape as of October 2026 and may not reflect subsequent FDA actions or guidance.

research.title: AI Versus Human-Led Triage in Primary Care and Emergency Settings: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2019-2026)
research.venue: Journal of Public Health and Community Medicine
research.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, registered in PROSPERO, evaluating diagnostic accuracy, operational efficiency, and safety of AI-assisted triage systems compared to traditional human-led triage across primary care and emergency settings from 2019 to 2026.
research.caveat: Meta-analysis of heterogeneous study designs and triage systems; generalisability may be limited by varying triage protocols and settings across included studies.

research.title: Clinical Safety Evaluation of LLM Assistants Using Decomposed LLM-as-Judges
research.finding: Developed a framework that decomposes hazards into auditable criteria applied by LLM judges, designed to provide a scalable risk-estimate input to ISO 14971 risk management. Evaluated using a user-facing women's health chatbot. The approach connects model failures to formal medical-device risk management.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The framework was evaluated on a single women's health chatbot; generalisability to other clinical domains and agent architectures is not established.

research.title: Expert Perspectives on US Regulatory Approaches to Large Language Models in Healthcare
research.finding: An interview series with Dr Shantanu Nundy, advisor in the office of the FDA Commissioner, exploring the challenge of regulating LLM-enabled medical AI, particularly where it extends beyond the usual boundaries of medical devices and challenges traditional regulatory frameworks.
research.caveat: Interview-based perspective article, not systematic analysis. Views expressed include those of an FDA advisor but do not represent official FDA policy.

research.title: HomePal: Passive Home Sensing System for Detecting Loneliness in Older Adults
research.venue: VCU College of Engineering / Emory University
research.finding: Researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University and Emory University developed HomePal, a passive home sensing system combining commercially available sensors to monitor movement, screen time, sleep, phone usage and vocal patterns. The system detects behavioral signatures associated with loneliness in older adults and reports results to a caregiving team, extending ambient home health monitoring from physical safety to mental health and social wellbeing.
research.caveat: The system is a research prototype; no clinical validation data has been published yet. Loneliness detection is based on behavioral correlates, not direct clinical assessment.

research.title: SAGE: Sensor-Augmented Grounding Engine for LLM-Powered Sleep Care Agent
research.finding: Presents SAGE, a sensor-augmented grounding engine that bridges the Data-Action Gap in sleep care by grounding LLM agents in personal wearable data. SAGE addresses three failure modes: static dashboards lacking context, rule-based agents relying on rigid scripts, and LLM agents without personal data grounding causing trust issues.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The system has not been validated in a clinical trial or with a large user study.

research.title: Vermont VDPOSA: Consumer Health Data Provisions and AI Transparency Requirements
research.finding: Vermont's Data Privacy and Online Surveillance Act (VDPOSA) takes effect January 1, 2028, with standalone consumer health data provisions applying regardless of general applicability thresholds. The law prohibits geofencing within 1,850 feet of healthcare facilities, requires consent before selling consumer health data, and includes AI transparency requirements.
research.caveat: The law does not take effect until 2028 and its enforcement mechanisms and interaction with existing state privacy laws remain to be tested.

research.title: LifeLong Digital Twin: A Unified Modeling Paradigm and Agent Harness for Event-Driven Lifelong Health State Trajectories
research.finding: Presents LifeLong Digital Twin, a unified modeling paradigm and agent harness for event-driven lifelong health state trajectories. The framework models health as a continuous state trajectory driven by discrete events (clinical encounters, self-reported symptoms, wearable data), enabling an agent to reason about a person's health history and future trajectories holistically rather than as isolated snapshots.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The framework is conceptual and has not been validated in a clinical deployment. The digital twin paradigm raises questions about model fidelity and the risks of acting on predicted trajectories that may not match individual physiology.

research.title: Evaluation of Symptom Checker Formats to Support Health Literacy and Trust in AI: Online Randomised Controlled Trial
research.finding: An online randomised controlled trial evaluating the impact of different symptom checker formats on symptom management knowledge, trust in AI symptom checkers, and accuracy of triage recommendations. The study addresses how the design and presentation of symptom checker outputs affects user comprehension and trust, which is critical for safe deployment of consumer-facing AI triage tools.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Online RCT with simulated scenarios may not reflect real-world symptom checker use. The specific formats tested may not generalise to all symptom checker platforms.

research.title: VitalAgent: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Reactive and Proactive Physiological Monitoring over Wearable Health Data
research.venue: arXiv (cs.AI) - University of Melbourne, Dartmouth, University of Auckland, Eindhoven University
research.finding: Presents VitalAgent, a tool-augmented agent architecture for both reactive (user-initiated) and proactive (system-initiated) physiological monitoring over wearable health data. The framework combines tool use, temporal reasoning and proactive alerting to address the gap between passive data dashboards and active health agents.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Evaluation details and performance metrics are not fully described in the abstract. Real-world deployment with actual patients is not demonstrated.

research.title: A Framework for Longitudinal Health AI Agents
research.finding: Presents a framework for designing AI agents that support longitudinal health tasks such as symptom management, behavior change and patient support. The framework draws on established conventions for follow-up, coherent reasoning and sustained alignment with individuals' goals to address the gap between current implementations and longitudinal care needs. The authors argue that most current implementations fall short of facilitating user intent and fostering accountability.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The framework is conceptual and has not been validated in a clinical deployment. Feasibility and scalability of the proposed design are not demonstrated.

research.title: EmoMed: An Emotionally-Aware Agent for Multimodal Medical Support with Real-Time Information Retrieval
research.finding: Presents EmoMed, an emotionally-aware agent for multimodal medical support with real-time information retrieval. The system integrates emotional awareness with medical knowledge retrieval, extending health agent design from purely clinical reasoning to affect-aware interaction. The architecture combines multimodal input processing, emotion recognition, and real-time medical information retrieval to provide contextually appropriate medical support.
research.caveat: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. The system is a research prototype and has not been validated in clinical trials. Emotional awareness in medical AI raises novel safety and ethical questions distinct from clinical accuracy alone.

research.title: Artificial Intelligence for Triage in Primary Care: A Scoping Review of Clinical Applicability
research.finding: A scoping review mapping 17 AI triage systems in primary care found most systems supported clinicians on diagnostic and referral tasks, but no system operated fully automatically without a clinician. Clinician performance improved when systems assisted imaging and ECG interpretation. The review covers the clinical applicability landscape of AI triage and addresses the gap between vendor claims of autonomy and the reality of clinician-assist deployment models.
research.caveat: Scoping review, not systematic review or meta-analysis. Heterogeneous systems and study designs make direct comparison difficult. The review may not capture all recently deployed systems.

research.title: Concordance Between an AI Self-Triage Programme and Physical Triage in the Emergency Department
research.finding: A study from Amsterdam UMC and OLVG Hospital evaluated concordance between an AI self-triage programme and physical triage in the emergency department. The study compares AI-assisted triage recommendations with in-person triage outcomes, providing real-world concordance data for AI triage tools deployed outside controlled vignette settings.
research.caveat: Single-centre study from the Netherlands. Concordance with physical triage is not the same as triage correctness or improved outcomes. Generalisability to other healthcare systems and triage protocols is not established.

freeTierDefaults.paidDefault: GPT-6 Sol (Plus / Pro / Business / Enterprise); GPT-6 Pro powered by GPT-6 Astra on the top tiers
freeTierDefaults.healthAccess: Health in ChatGPT is free for logged-in US users on Free, Go, Plus and Pro, on web and iOS. A free user can connect Apple Health and supported US medical records and get grounded, cited health answers with no separate fee. OpenAI published no separate per-plan limit on the Health experience itself; free users are bounded by the general chat limits.
freeTierDefaults.freeTierLimits: Unlimited text chats with GPT-6, subject to abuse guardrails. Separate caps on uploads, image generation, voice, data analysis and Codex. Free users get the Think toggle but no Medium / High / Extra High / Pro reasoning levels, and no access to GPT-6 Pro or Astra.
freeTierDefaults.healthNote: OpenAI's own system-card addendum on the October 29, 2026 GPT-6 Luna update - the build that applies to Free and Go users - reports higher factual-error rates on health and wellness questions than the October 7 build. So the free tier and the paid tier are not merely different in capability on health; the free model was, for a period, measurably weaker on exactly the questions a patient asks.
freeTierDefaults.notes: A patient asking a health question on a free ChatGPT account is talking to GPT-6 Luna. Paid tiers get GPT-6 Sol with higher reasoning levels and, at the top, Astra.
freeTierDefaults.conflict: OpenAI's own pages disagree on the version label for the free default. The help centre says 'GPT-5.6 Luna is becoming the default model for Free and Go users' (updated ~Oct 30) and the Free Tier FAQ says free users have access to GPT-5.6 Luna (updated ~Nov 6), while the live pricing page lists GPT-6 Luna as available on Free and GPT-5.6 Luna as not available on Free. Resolved to GPT-6 Luna: the pricing page is live and current, the October 7 release note says 'Free and Go use GPT-6 Luna', and the October 29 model update is scoped to Free and Go users - which is only possible if free users were already on GPT-6. The help-centre copy looks like prose that has not been refreshed since the GPT-6 rollout. Both candidate labels are Luna-tier models, so the practical difference is the generation number, not the tier.

freeTierDefaults.freeDefault: AI Mode: Gemini 3.5 Flash (global default since May 19, 2026). AI Overviews: Gemini 3 was the last explicit vendor default (Jan 27, 2026), with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite now routing some Search queries

freeTierDefaults.healthAccess: No health-specific model and no health-specific free-tier limits are published. Google's published position is that health results in Search come from advanced AI and health-focused advancements on Gemini models that make AI Overviews more clinically factual, and that people with the most complex health questions should move into AI Mode. There is no dedicated health model and no paid/free contrast beyond Argon's availability.
freeTierDefaults.freeTierLimits: Argon carries daily usage limits for subscribers. Google publishes no limits tied to health queries.
freeTierDefaults.healthNote: For a free consumer, the hardest health questions land on Gemini 3.5 Flash in AI Mode — while an AI Pro/Ultra subscriber can escalate to Argon. Google separately published an end-to-end framework for evaluating AI on health scenarios (accuracy, safety, usefulness) with clinician review on Nov 4, 2026, and partners with national medical institutions for locally calibrated health sourcing.
freeTierDefaults.notes: AI Mode is the more consequential surface for a patient: Google set Gemini 3.5 Flash as the default in AI Mode for everyone globally at I/O 2026, and merged AI Overviews into that flow. Since July 2026 Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite has also been rolling out in Google Search for high-volume, latency-sensitive queries.
freeTierDefaults.conflict: The AI Overviews default is the soft point. Google's last explicit, vendor-stated default for AI Overviews is Gemini 3 (Jan 27, 2026), while at I/O 2026 Google merged AI Overviews into AI Mode and moved the combined flow onto Gemini 3.5 Flash. Google has not published a fresh AI-Overviews-specific default statement, and it states plainly that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use different models. So this entry reports the last explicit vendor default (Gemini 3) alongside the merged-flow reality (Gemini 3.5 Flash) rather than asserting one. Google also never labels which model wrote a given answer — routing is server-side and per query — so any single-answer model claim is unsupported.
